title: The Instruction of Amen-em-apt, son of Kanakht (Chapter 1)
ask_addressed: Quote the Egyptian primary texts that threads depend on: the Instruction of Amenemope (chapters 1-3, 9-10 compared by scholars with Proverbs)
quote: Give your ears, hear the sayings, give your heart to understand them.
summary: Opening charge of the Instruction. Compare Proverbs 22:17 'Incline your ear and listen to the words of the sages'. Both open by commanding the hearer to listen and to store the words within.
limits: Modern English rendering by one translator, not a scholarly edition with apparatus; verify against Griffith JEA 12 (1926) or Lichtheim.

title: The Instruction of Amen-em-apt, son of Kanakht (Chapter 2)
ask_addressed: Quote the Egyptian primary texts that threads depend on: the Instruction of Amenemope (chapters 1-3, 9-10 compared by scholars with Proverbs)
quote: Beware of robbing a poor wretch, of attacking a cripple.
summary: Chapter 2 forbids robbing the poor. The usual comparison is Proverbs 22:22 'Do not rob the wretched because they are wretched'.
limits: The two share the prohibition and the vocabulary of 'wretched/poor' in translation only; Ruffle accepts this pair, Brunet counts it among five of eleven. Not proof of borrowing.

title: The Instruction of Amen-em-apt, son of Kanakht (Chapter 3 and Chapter 9)
ask_addressed: Quote the Egyptian primary texts that threads depend on: the Instruction of Amenemope (chapters 1-3, 9-10 compared by scholars with Proverbs)
quote: Do not befriend the heated man, nor approach him for conversation.
summary: Chapter 9 warns against the 'heated man' (hot-tempered); chapter 3 has 'Do not start a quarrel with a hot-mouthed man'. Compare Proverbs 22:24 'Make no friendship with an angry man'.
limits: Ruffle (p. 63-64) notes some parallels only 'work' when Proverbs is set beside an Amenemope passage with a large gap between them.

title: The Instruction of Amen-em-apt, son of Kanakht (Chapter 6)
ask_addressed: Quote the Egyptian primary texts that threads depend on: the Instruction of Amenemope (chapters 1-3, 9-10 compared by scholars with Proverbs)
quote: Do not move the markers on the borders of fields.
summary: Boundary-marker prohibition. Compare Proverbs 22:28 'Do not remove the ancient boundary stone' and 23:10. The boundary-marker law is also widely attested outside both texts.
limits: Boundary-stone prohibitions are a stock motif of ancient Near Eastern law; the parallel alone shows no route.

title: The Instruction of Amen-em-apt, son of Kanakht (Chapter 30, epilogue)
ask_addressed: Quote the Egyptian primary texts that threads depend on: the Instruction of Amenemope (chapters 1-3, 9-10 compared by scholars with Proverbs)
quote: Look to these thirty chapters : they inform, they educate, they are the foremost of all books
summary: The epilogue names the thirty chapters; the Hebrew in Proverbs 22:20 (shilshom, 'threefold' in JPS; 'excellent things' in KJV) has been emended to 'thirty' by those arguing dependence.
limits: The Hebrew reading of 22:20 is uncertain; the emendation is a scholarly proposal, not the transmitted text. Ruffle discusses it as the crux of the debate.

title: The Teaching of Amenemope and its Connection with the Book of Proverbs
venue: Tyndale Bulletin (Tyndale Biblical Archaeology Lecture, delivered 19 June 1975)
ask_addressed: Quote the Egyptian primary texts that threads depend on: the Instruction of Amenemope (chapters 1-3, 9-10 compared by scholars with Proverbs)
quote: I confess to some doubt about the existence of a direct connection between Proverbs and Amenemope.
summary: A reviewing Egyptologist counts roughly 11 of 24 verses as matched in subject and finds this 'not wholly conclusive' evidence of direct borrowing; notes Amenemope's central themes (hothead vs quiet man) are absent from Proverbs.
limits: Ruffle (the lecture's own position, an evangelical venue) also defends a Solomonic compiler, so is not neutral on date; he still allows 'a case could be argued for dependence' from cumulative parallels.

text.edition: Tyndale Bulletin, lecture text as PDF (doi 10.53751/001c.30616)

composition.basis: Ruffle: 'a date for the composition before 1,000 B.C.', an XVIIIth Dynasty date 'acceptable' on Cairo/Stockholm copies

text.witness: BM 10474: 'can be dated between the XXIInd and XXVIth Dynasties, i.e. between 950 and 650 B. C.'; Cairo ostracon late XXIst or early XXIInd Dynasty (Cerny)

title: Religion and Thought in Ancient Egypt: Great Hymn to the Aten (night strophe)
venue: Scribner; archive.org scan of the Morse Lectures
ask_addressed: Quote the Egyptian primary texts that threads depend on: ... the Great Hymn to the Aten (Amarna, c. 1350 BCE)
quote: Every lion cometh forth from his den, All serpents, they sting.
summary: Night strophe: darkness releases lions and serpents. Compare Psalm 104:20-21 'all the beasts of the forest do creep forth. The young lions roar'.
limits: Resemblance in motif; Lichtheim and others deny specific interdependence.

composition.basis: Akhenaten's reign, mid-14th century BCE, per Wikipedia 'Great Hymn to the Aten' ('Composed in the middle of the 14th century BC'); exact reign dates not read from an Egyptological source here

text.witness: Copied on the wall of the tomb of Ay at Amarna (Southern Tomb 25); shorter versions in other Amarna tombs

title: The Decrees of Memphis and Canopus, vol. II: The Rosetta Stone (English rendering of the Demotic text)
venue: Archive.org scan (Books on Egypt and Chaldaea series)
ask_addressed: Quote the Egyptian primary texts that threads depend on: ... the Rosetta Stone and Canopus Decree (Egyptian hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek in one text)
quote: inscribed upon a stele of hard stone in the writing of the divine words, and in the writing of the books, and in the writing of the Greeks
summary: The decree orders its own publication in three scripts: hieroglyphic ('divine words'), Demotic ('the books') and Greek. This is the text's own statement of its trilingual form.
limits: Budge's 1904 rendering of the Demotic, with OCR; the Greek version's wording differs slightly. Modern translations (Simpson, Quirke-Andrews) exist.

text.work: Rosetta Stone decree (Memphis decree of Ptolemy V Epiphanes)
text.locator: Closing clause of the Demotic text
text.language: Demotic Egyptian, quoted in English (also on the stone in hieroglyphic and Greek)
text.edition: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Decrees of Memphis and Canopus, vol. II: The Rosetta Stone (London, 1904), English rendering of the Demotic text

composition.basis: Dated in the decree itself to Ptolemy V's 9th year (4 Xandikos = 18 Mechir); 196 BCE per Wikipedia 'Rosetta Stone' (created 196 BC)

text.witness: Stele of granodiorite, found 1799 near Rashid, now British Museum (inventory 'EA 24' per Wikipedia); Budge's 1904 text predates the 'granodiorite' identification

title: The Decrees of Memphis and Canopus, vol. III: The Stele of Canopus
venue: Archive.org scan (Books on Egypt and Chaldaea series)

quote: it shall be cut upon a stele of stone or bronze in the writing of the House of Life, and in the writing of the books, and in the writing of the Greeks
summary: Like the Rosetta decree, the Canopus decree orders itself engraved in three scripts, a century earlier (238 BCE vs 196 BCE).
limits: Budge's rendering; the several copies differ in how they list the scripts ('hieroglyphic characters, and in Egyptian and Greek characters' in one).

quote: Hail to thee, Atum! Hail to thee, Kheprer! Who himself became
summary: Breasted calls it 'the earliest Sun-hymn which we possess'; Egypt is the 'Horus-eye' the god adorned.
limits: 1912 translation; Breasted's rendering of Pyr. §1479, not the modern Allen or Faulkner. Date of the underlying spell not fixed.

title: Religion and Thought in Ancient Egypt: the Memphite theology (heart and tongue)
venue: Scribner; archive.org scan of the Morse Lectures
ask_addressed: Quote the Egyptian primary texts that threads depend on: ... a Pyramid Text spell, and the Memphite Theology
quote: Every divine word came into existence by the thought of the heart and the commandment of the tongue.
summary: Ptah creates through 'heart and tongue': thought conceived in the heart, spoken by the tongue.
limits: Breasted's translation of a mutilated text, whose 1912 dating (Old Kingdom) is now widely rejected.

text.locator: Lines on the heart and tongue (Breasted p. 45)
text.edition: J. H. Breasted, Development of Religion and Thought in Ancient Egypt (1912), pp. 44-45

composition.basis: Disputed: Breasted, Erman, Sethe, Junker put it in the Old Kingdom; Junge and most later scholars date it to the 25th Dynasty (Wikipedia 'Shabaka Stone'); 'cannot predate the Nineteenth Dynasty' (Van De Mieroop, as quoted). Range spans the later views only

text.witness: Shabaka Stone, black granite slab, British Museum (BM 498 per Breasted's footnote), carved late 8th c. BCE as a copy of a 'worm-eaten' papyrus; later reused as a millstone

title: Shabaka Stone (Wikipedia, section on dating)
ask_addressed: Quote the Egyptian primary texts that threads depend on: ... a Pyramid Text spell, and the Memphite Theology
quote: Friedrich Junge and most other scholars since then have argued that the monument was produced in the Twenty-fifth Dynasty
summary: Records the shift from Old Kingdom dating (Breasted, Erman, Sethe) to the 25th Dynasty (Junge); the stone itself claims to copy an older worm-eaten papyrus.
limits: Wikipedia secondary; Bodine 2009 not opened. Not a dating by itself.
